title: Lesson 78 - Let Me Walk You Through the Proposal

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Let me walk you through the proposal in five parts: the problem, the pilot design, the expected benefit, the main risks and the decision I’m asking for today.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: Before you begin, are you asking us to approve evening bookings?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: No. I need you to hear me out through the risk controls first. I’m asking only whether the draft is complete enough for a resource review.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: That distinction helps. What problem are we actually trying to solve?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: The problem we’re trying to solve is uncertainty. We receive after-hours inquiries, but we don’t know the real demand, operating cost or effect on the next morning.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: So the proposal is a way to learn, not a promise to create a new revenue line.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Correct. The proposal has three operating parts: four Tuesday trials, pre-booked groups of no more than fourteen and a ninety-minute service window with a limited drinks-and-pastries menu.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: Why Tuesdays? Friday inquiries have been more common.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Let me finish this part, and then I’ll show the day comparison. Tuesdays reduce conflict with our busiest daytime preparation, but that assumption still needs the resource sheet.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: All right. Continue with the conditions before we debate the preferred day.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: If we were to run four bounded trials, we could compare actual setup, service, cleanup and next-morning effects without committing to a recurring schedule.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: The main benefit would be better evidence. What is the main operational risk?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: The main risk is hidden labor. A ninety-minute booking could become a four-hour burden once preparation, closing and recovery are counted.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: There is also cancellation risk. If a group cancels late, we may have scheduled people and prepared food without useful demand evidence.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: Agreed. The controls would be a booking deposit, a fixed order deadline, no hot-kitchen service, two named staff members and a stop review after the second trial.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: I would add a next-morning check. If either closer is also on the opening shift, the trial should not go ahead unless the schedule has been adjusted.

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: That might work if the schedule can protect the recovery window. I’ll add it as a condition rather than assume a manager can always find cover.

lines.speaker: Owen
lines.text: What exactly are you asking us to decide at the end of this presentation?

lines.speaker: Rosa
lines.text: I’m not asking you to agree that evening bookings are the right direction; I’m asking you to confirm that the proposal states enough conditions to price and staff honestly.

lines.speaker: Malik
lines.text: Then my answer is yes with two revisions: show the day comparison and make next-morning coverage a required resource, not a hopeful note.
